label: Crito
title: Crito
paragraphs: SOCRATES: Why have you come at this hour, Crito? Isn't it still early?
CRITO: Very early.
SOCRATES: About what time?
CRITO: Just before dawn.
SOCRATES: I'm surprised the prison guard was willing to let you in.
CRITO: He is used to me by now, Socrates, I come here so often; and besides, I have done him a kindness.
SOCRATES: Have you just come, or have you been here a while?
CRITO: A fair while.
SOCRATES: Then why didn't you wake me at once, instead of sitting beside me in silence?

CRITO: By Zeus, Socrates, I would not want to be awake myself in such sleeplessness and grief. I have been wondering at you for some time, seeing how sweetly you sleep; and I kept from waking you on purpose, so that you might pass the time as pleasantly as possible. Often before, through your whole life, I have thought you happy in your temper, but never so much as in this present misfortune, seeing how easily and calmly you bear it.
SOCRATES: Well, Crito, it would be out of tune for a man of my age to be upset because he must now die.
CRITO: Other men of your age are caught in such misfortunes, Socrates, and their age does nothing to keep them from being upset at what has come to them.
SOCRATES: That is so. But why have you come so early?
CRITO: I bring news, Socrates, hard news — not for you, it seems, but for me and for all your friends hard and heavy; and I think I will bear it as heavily as any of them.
SOCRATES: What news? Has the ship come in from Delos, the one whose arrival means I must die?

CRITO: It has not come in yet, but I think it will be here today, from the report of some people who have come from Sunium and left it there. It is clear from what they say that it will be here today; and so tomorrow, Socrates, your life must end.
SOCRATES: Well, Crito, may it be for the best. If this is what pleases the gods, so be it. But I don't think it will come today.
CRITO: What makes you think so?
SOCRATES: I will tell you. I am to die, I believe, on the day after the ship arrives.
CRITO: So those in charge of these things say.
SOCRATES: Then I don't think it will come on the day now beginning, but on the next. I judge by a dream I had a little while ago, in the night; and it may be that you did well not to wake me.
CRITO: What was the dream?
SOCRATES: I thought a woman came to me, beautiful and fair to look at, dressed in white, and she called me and said: Socrates, ‘on the third day you will come to fertile Phthia.’
CRITO: A strange dream, Socrates.
SOCRATES: No, a clear one, as it seems to me, Crito.

CRITO: Too clear, it seems. But my dear Socrates, even now, listen to me and save yourself. For me, if you die, it will be more than one misfortune. Besides losing a friend such as I will never find again, I will also seem to many people, who do not know you and me well, to have neglected you, when I could have saved you if I had been willing to spend the money. And what reputation could be more shameful than that of valuing money above one's friends? Most people will not believe that you yourself refused to leave this place, though we were eager for it.

SOCRATES: But why, my dear Crito, should we care so much about what most people think? The most reasonable people, who deserve more of our attention, will believe that things were done just as they are done.

CRITO: But you see, Socrates, that one has to care about the opinion of the many too. What is happening now makes it plain that the many are able to do not the smallest of evils but very nearly the greatest, if a man is slandered among them.

SOCRATES: If only the many were able to do the greatest evils, Crito, so that they might also be able to do the greatest goods! That would be well. As it is, they can do neither. They cannot make a man wise or foolish; they do whatever comes to hand.

CRITO: Let that be as you say. But tell me this, Socrates. Surely you are not worrying about me and your other friends — that if you leave here, the informers will make trouble for us for having stolen you away, and we will be forced to lose all our property, or a great deal of money, or suffer something else besides? If you are afraid of anything like that, let it go. It is only right that we should run this risk to save you, and a greater one if need be. Listen to me, and do not refuse.
SOCRATES: I am worrying about that, Crito, and about many other things.

CRITO: Then do not be afraid of that. It is not even a large sum that certain people want for saving you and getting you out of here. And then, do you not see how cheap these informers are? It would not take much money to deal with them. My money is at your service, and I think it is enough. And then, if out of some concern for me you think you should not spend mine, there are these foreigners here, ready to spend theirs. One of them has brought enough money for this very purpose, Simmias the Theban; and Cebes is ready too, and a great many others. So, as I say, do not give up on saving yourself out of fear of that. And do not let it trouble you, as you said in court, that if you went away you would not know what to do with yourself. In many other places, wherever you go, they will welcome you. And if you want to go to Thessaly, I have friends there who will think very highly of you and keep you safe, so that no one in Thessaly will trouble you.

Besides, Socrates, I do not think that what you are doing is even just: betraying yourself when you could be saved. You are hurrying to bring on yourself the very thing your enemies would hurry to bring on you, and did, when they wanted to destroy you. And more than that, I think you are betraying your own sons. You could bring them up and educate them, and instead you will go away and leave them, and as far as you are concerned they will fare as chance decides; and they will probably meet with what orphans usually meet with when they have lost their parents. Either one should not have children, or one should see the trouble through with them, bringing them up and educating them. But you seem to me to be choosing the easiest way. One ought to choose what a good and brave man would choose, especially if one claims to have cared for virtue all one's life. I am ashamed, for you and for us your friends. I am afraid it will be thought that this whole business of yours was carried through by some cowardice on our part: the case coming into court when it need not have come, and the way the trial itself was conducted, and now this last act, the absurd ending of the whole affair — that we will be thought to have let the chance slip through some baseness and cowardice of ours, since we did not save you and you did not save yourself, when it was possible and could be done, if we had been of the least use. See to it, Socrates, that this does not turn out to be shameful as well as bad, for you and for us. Make up your mind — or rather, the time for making it up is past; it should be made up. And there is only one plan. Everything must be done this coming night. If we wait any longer it cannot be done; it will no longer be possible. I beg you, Socrates, listen to me, and do not refuse.

SOCRATES: My dear Crito, your eagerness is worth a great deal, if there is some rightness in it. If not, the greater it is, the harder it is to deal with. So we must consider whether this should be done or not. For I am not only now but always the kind of man who is persuaded by nothing in me except the argument that seems best to me when I reason it out. I cannot throw away the arguments I used before, now that this has happened to me. They look much the same to me, and I respect and honor the same ones as before. And unless we have better ones to offer now, be sure that I will not give way to you — not even if the power of the many should try to frighten us with more bogeymen than it has now, as if we were children, sending chains and deaths and the seizing of property against us.

How then can we look into this most reasonably? Suppose we first take up the argument you make about opinions. Was it right or not, what we always used to say: that one should pay attention to some opinions and not to others? Or was it right before I had to die, but now it has become clear that it was said idly, for the sake of talking, and was really play and nonsense? I am eager to examine it together with you, Crito, and see whether it will look any different to me now that I am in this position, or the same; and whether we shall say goodbye to it or be persuaded by it. It used to be said, I think, by people who thought they were talking sense, just as I said a moment ago: that of the opinions people hold, some should be highly valued and others not. By the gods, Crito, does that not seem to you well said? For you, in all human likelihood, are in no danger of dying tomorrow, and the present misfortune should not lead you astray. Consider, then. Does it not seem to you rightly said that one should not honor all the opinions people hold, but some and not others; and not the opinions of everyone, but of some and not others? What do you say? Is that not well said?
CRITO: It is.
SOCRATES: That we should honor the good ones, and not the bad?
CRITO: Yes.
SOCRATES: And the good ones are those of the wise, the bad ones those of the foolish?
CRITO: Of course.

SOCRATES: Come then, what used we to say about cases like this? A man in athletic training, who makes it his business — does he pay attention to the praise and blame and opinion of every man, or only of the one man who is a doctor or a trainer?
CRITO: Only of the one.
SOCRATES: So he should fear the blame and welcome the praise of that one man, and not of the many.
CRITO: Clearly.
SOCRATES: Then he must act and exercise, and eat and drink, in the way that seems good to the one man, the supervisor who understands, rather than in the way that seems good to all the others.
CRITO: That is so.
SOCRATES: Very well. And if he disobeys the one, and dishonors his opinion and his praises, and honors the words of the many who understand nothing, won't he come to some harm?
CRITO: Of course he will.
SOCRATES: What is this harm? Where does it tend, and what does it affect in the man who disobeys?
CRITO: His body, clearly. That is what it ruins.

SOCRATES: Well said. And is it not the same with everything else, Crito, not to go through it all? And especially with the just and the unjust, the shameful and the honorable, the good and the bad, which are what we are now deliberating about — should we follow the opinion of the many, and fear it, or the opinion of the one, if there is someone who understands, before whom we should feel more shame and fear than before all the others? If we do not follow him, we shall corrupt and maim that part of us which, as we said, is made better by what is just and is destroyed by what is unjust. Or is there nothing in that?
CRITO: I think there is, Socrates.

SOCRATES: Come then. If we ruin the part that is made better by what is healthy and corrupted by what is diseased, because we do not obey the opinion of those who understand, is life worth living for us once it is corrupted? And that part is the body, is it not?
CRITO: Yes.
SOCRATES: Is life worth living for us, then, with a wretched and corrupted body?
CRITO: Not at all.

SOCRATES: But is it worth living with that part corrupted which the unjust maims and the just benefits? Or do we think that part of us, whatever it is, which injustice and justice have to do with, is of less account than the body?
CRITO: Not at all.
SOCRATES: More precious, rather?
CRITO: Much more.

SOCRATES: Then, my good friend, we must not care so much what the many will say of us, but what he will say who understands about the just and the unjust, the one man, and the truth itself. So first of all, you bring the matter in wrongly when you say we must care about the opinion of the many concerning what is just and honorable and good and their opposites. But then, someone might say, the many are able to put us to death.
CRITO: That is clear too. Someone might well say it, Socrates.

SOCRATES: That's true. But, my dear friend, the argument we have just gone through still seems to me the same as it was before. And look at this one too, and see whether it still stands for us or not: It is not living that matters most, but living well.
CRITO: It still stands.
SOCRATES: And that living well and living honorably and living justly are the same thing — does that stand or not?
CRITO: It stands.

SOCRATES: Then starting from what we have agreed, we must consider this: whether it is just for me to try to leave here when the Athenians have not released me, or not just. If it appears just, let us try; if not, let us give it up. As for the considerations you mention, about spending money, and reputation, and the bringing up of children, I suspect, Crito, that these are really the concerns of those who lightly put people to death, and would bring them back to life again if they could, without any sense at all — of these same many. But for us, since the argument so decides, I suspect there is nothing else to consider but what we said just now: whether we shall be acting justly in paying money and giving thanks to those who are to get me out of here, and in getting out and being got out ourselves, or whether in truth we shall be doing wrong in doing all this. And if it appears that we would be acting unjustly, I suspect we must not take into account whether we shall have to die if we stay here and keep quiet, or suffer anything else whatever, rather than do wrong.
CRITO: I think what you say is right, Socrates. But consider what we are to do.

SOCRATES: Let us look into it together, my good friend, and if you have any objection to what I say, make it, and I will be persuaded by you. If not, my dear friend, stop telling me the same thing over and over, that I ought to leave here against the will of the Athenians. I think it very important to act in this with your consent, and not against your will. Now see whether the starting point of the inquiry satisfies you, and try to answer what I ask as you really think.
CRITO: I will try.

SOCRATES: Do we say that one must never willingly do wrong, in any way? Or that one may do wrong in one way and not in another? Or is doing wrong never good or honorable, as we have often agreed in the past? Or have all those former agreements of ours been poured away in these last few days? Have we, Crito, old men as we are, been talking earnestly with each other all this time and never noticed that we were no better than children? Or is it, above all, just as we used to say then: whether the many agree or not, and whether we must suffer harder things than these or lighter ones, doing wrong is in every way evil and shameful for the one who does it? Do we say that or not?
CRITO: We do.
SOCRATES: Then one must never do wrong.
CRITO: Of course not.
SOCRATES: Nor do wrong in return when one is wronged, as the many think, since one must never do wrong.
CRITO: It appears not.
SOCRATES: Well then: should one do harm, Crito, or not?
CRITO: Surely not, Socrates.
SOCRATES: And to do harm in return when one has been harmed — is that just, as the many say, or not just?
CRITO: Not at all.
SOCRATES: For doing harm to people is no different from doing them wrong.
CRITO: That's true.

SOCRATES: Then one must not do wrong in return, or do harm to any human being, whatever one suffers at their hands. And take care, Crito, that in agreeing to this you are not agreeing against your real opinion. For I know that few people hold this view, or ever will. And between those who hold it and those who do not there is no common ground; they are bound to despise one another when they see one another's decisions. So consider very carefully whether you share this view with me and agree, and whether we should begin our deliberation from here: that it is never right to do wrong, or to do wrong in return, or, when one is harmed, to defend oneself by doing harm back. Or do you draw away, and not share this starting point? I have thought so for a long time, and I think so still. But if you have come to think otherwise, say so and teach me. If you stand by what we said before, hear the next point.
CRITO: I do stand by it, and I agree. Go on.
SOCRATES: Then I will say the next thing, or rather ask it. When a man has agreed with someone to do something, and it is just, should he do it or cheat him of it?
CRITO: He should do it.

SOCRATES: Then look at what follows. If we go away from here without persuading the city, are we doing harm to anyone, and to those we should least harm, or not? And are we standing by what we agreed to, it being just, or not?
CRITO: I cannot answer your question, Socrates. I do not understand it.

SOCRATES: Then look at it this way. Suppose that, as we were about to run away from here, or whatever one should call it, the Laws and the commonwealth of the city came and stood before us and asked: Tell us, Socrates, what do you have in mind to do? By this act that you are attempting, what else do you intend but to destroy us, the Laws, and the whole city, as far as it lies with you? Or do you think a city can go on existing, and not be overturned, in which the judgments that are given have no force, but are made void and destroyed by private persons? What shall we say, Crito, to this and to other things like it? For there is a great deal that one could say, especially an orator, on behalf of this law that is being destroyed, the law that requires judgments once given to be binding. Or shall we say to them: Yes, for the city wronged us, and did not judge the case rightly? Shall we say that, or what?
CRITO: That, by Zeus, Socrates.

SOCRATES: Then what if the Laws say: Socrates, was that the agreement between us and you? Or was it to abide by whatever judgments the city gives? And if we were surprised at their saying this, perhaps they would say: Socrates, do not be surprised at what we say, but answer, since you are used to dealing in question and answer. Come, what charge do you bring against us and the city, that you are trying to destroy us? Did we not, first of all, bring you into being? Was it not through us that your father took your mother and begot you? Tell us, then: those of us that are the laws of marriage — do you find some fault with them, as not being good? I find no fault, I would say. Or with those about the bringing up of a child once he is born, and the education in which you too were educated? Did those of us who are set over this not give the right orders when we told your father to educate you in music and physical training? You did, I would say. Very well. And since you were born and brought up and educated, can you say, to begin with, that you were not ours, our offspring and our slave, you and your forefathers too? And if that is so, do you think that what is just is the same for you as for us, and that whatever we try to do to you, it is just for you to do the same back to us? Toward your father you were not on an equal footing as to what is just, or toward your master if you had one, so as to do back to them whatever was done to you — to answer back when you were scolded, or strike back when you were struck, or any of the many things of that kind. And will you be allowed to do so toward your country and the Laws? So that if we try to destroy you, thinking it just, you in turn will try, as far as you are able, to destroy us, the Laws, and your country, and will say that in doing this you act justly — you, the man who truly cares about virtue? Or are you so wise that you have failed to see that your country is more precious than your mother and your father and all your other forefathers, more to be revered and more holy, and held in higher esteem both among the gods and among human beings of sense? That you must reverence your country, and give way to her and soothe her when she is angry, more than you would a father; and either persuade her, or do what she commands; and suffer in silence whatever she orders you to suffer, whether it is to be beaten or to be put in chains; and if she leads you to war to be wounded or killed, you must do it, and that is what is just; and you must not give way, or retreat, or leave your post, but in war and in court and everywhere you must do what your city and your country command, or else persuade her where justice lies? And that it is not holy to use force against a mother or a father, and far less against your country? What shall we say to this, Crito? That the Laws speak the truth, or not?
CRITO: I think they do.

SOCRATES: Consider then, Socrates, the Laws might say, whether we are right in saying that what you are now trying to do to us is not just. We brought you into being, brought you up, educated you, and gave you and all the other citizens a share in every fine thing we could. And yet we proclaim, by giving the permission, that any Athenian who wishes, once he has come of age and has seen the affairs of the city and us, the Laws, may take what is his and go wherever he likes, if we do not please him. Not one of us Laws stands in the way or forbids it. Whether one of you wishes to go to a colony, if we and the city do not please him, or to go and live as a foreigner somewhere else, he may go wherever he likes and keep what is his. But whoever of you stays, seeing the way we give judgment and manage the city in other respects, has by then, we say, agreed with us in deed to do whatever we command. And we say that the one who does not obey does wrong three times over: because he does not obey us who gave him birth; because he does not obey us who brought him up; and because, having agreed to obey us, he neither obeys nor persuades us if we are doing something that is not right. And yet we put it before him, and do not harshly order him to do what we command; we allow him one of two things, either to persuade us or to obey; and he does neither.

These are the charges, Socrates, to which we say you too will be open if you do what you have in mind — and you not least among the Athenians, but most of all. And if I said: Why so? perhaps they would justly rebuke me, saying that I more than any Athenian have made this agreement with them. They would say: Socrates, we have strong proofs that we and the city pleased you. You would never have stayed at home in it more than all other Athenians if it had not pleased you more than it pleased them. You never left the city to see a festival, except once to the Isthmus, nor to go anywhere else, except on military service somewhere; you never made any other journey abroad, as other people do; no desire ever seized you to know another city or other laws. We were enough for you, and our city. So firmly did you choose us, and agree to live as a citizen under us; and besides all this you had children in the city, which shows that it pleased you. And then, at the trial itself, you could have proposed exile as your penalty if you wished, and have done then with the city's consent what you are now attempting against her will. But then you put on a fine show of not being upset if you had to die; you chose death, you said, before exile. And now you are not ashamed of those words, and have no regard for us, the Laws, since you are trying to destroy us. You are doing what the lowest slave would do, trying to run away in breach of the compacts and agreements by which you agreed with us to live as a citizen. First, then, answer us this: are we telling the truth when we say that you agreed, in deed and not in word, to live as a citizen under us, or is it not true? What are we to say to that, Crito? Must we not agree?
CRITO: We must, Socrates.

SOCRATES: Then what else are you doing, they would say, but breaking your compacts and agreements with us? You did not make them under compulsion, or because you were deceived, or because you were forced to decide in a short time. You had seventy years, in which you could have gone away if we did not please you, or if the agreements did not seem to you just. But you did not prefer Lacedaemon or Crete, which you are always saying have good laws, or any other city, Greek or foreign. You were away from this one less than the lame, the blind and the other maimed. So much more than other Athenians did the city please you, and so, clearly, did we, the Laws; for whom would a city please without its laws? And now will you not stand by what you agreed? You will, Socrates, if you listen to us; and you will not make yourself ridiculous by leaving the city.

For consider: if you break these agreements and go wrong in any of these ways, what good will you do yourself or your friends? That your friends will themselves be in danger of exile, and of losing their city or their property, is fairly clear. And you yourself, first of all, if you go to one of the nearest cities, to Thebes or to Megara — for both have good laws — you will come as an enemy, Socrates, to their government; and all who care for their own cities will look at you with suspicion, thinking you a destroyer of the laws. And you will confirm the judges in their opinion, so that they will seem to have judged the case rightly. For anyone who is a destroyer of laws may well be thought a destroyer of the young and the foolish. Will you then keep away from cities with good laws, and from the most orderly of men? And if you do that, will your life be worth living? Or will you go up to them, and be shameless enough to talk with them — and say what, Socrates? What you said here, that virtue and justice are what is worth most to human beings, and lawfulness and the laws? Do you not think that this conduct of Socrates will look unseemly? You must think so. Or will you leave these places and go to Crito's friends in Thessaly? There, to be sure, there is the greatest disorder and license, and perhaps they would enjoy hearing how comically you ran away from prison, wrapped in some disguise, a peasant's leather cloak or one of the other things runaways dress up in, and with your appearance changed. But will no one say that an old man, with probably only a little time left to live, had the face to cling so greedily to life, and broke the greatest laws to do it? Perhaps not, if you offend no one. Otherwise, Socrates, you will hear many things said that are unworthy of you. So you will live by fawning on everyone and being their slave. And doing what, except feasting in Thessaly, as if you had traveled to Thessaly for a dinner? And those talks about justice and the rest of virtue — where will they be then? Or is it for your children's sake that you want to live, to bring them up and educate them? What then? Will you take them to Thessaly and bring them up and educate them there, and make foreigners of them, so that they may have that to thank you for as well? Or not that, but they will be brought up here, and will be better brought up and educated because you are alive, though you are not with them? Your friends will take care of them. Will they take care of them if you go away to Thessaly, and not if you go away to Hades? If those who call themselves your friends are of any use at all, you must believe they will.

No, Socrates. Listen to us who brought you up, and do not put children, or life, or anything else before what is just, so that when you come to Hades you may have all this to say in your defense to those who rule there. For if you do this thing, it does not appear better or more just or more holy for you here, or for any of yours; and it will not be better for you when you arrive there. As it is, if you go, you will go away wronged, not by us, the Laws, but by men. But if you escape after so shamefully doing wrong in return and harm in return, breaking your own agreements and compacts with us, and doing harm to those you should least harm — yourself, your friends, your country and us — then we will be angry with you while you live, and there our brothers, the Laws in Hades, will not receive you kindly, knowing that you tried to destroy us as far as it lay with you. Do not let Crito persuade you to do what he says, rather than us.

This, my dear friend Crito, be sure of it, is what I seem to hear, as those in the Corybantic frenzy seem to hear the flutes; and the sound of these words hums in me and makes me unable to hear any others. Be sure that, as far as I can see now, if you speak against this, you will speak in vain. Still, if you think you can do any good, speak.
CRITO: No, Socrates, I have nothing to say.
SOCRATES: Then let it be, Crito, and let us act in this way, since this is the way the god leads.

divergences.phrase: οὐ τὸ ζῆν περὶ πλείστου ποιητέον ἀλλὰ τὸ εὖ ζῆν
divergences.older: not life, but a good life, is to be chiefly valued
divergences.lectio: It is not living that matters most, but living well.
divergences.note: The Greek uses the verb twice, 'to live' and 'to live well', and the edition keeps the verb. The next line says what 'well' means: honorably and justly. 'A good life' in current English suggests comfort, which is the opposite of the point.

divergences.phrase: οὔτε ἄρα ἀνταδικεῖν δεῖ οὔτε κακῶς ποιεῖν οὐδένα ἀνθρώπων
divergences.older: Then we ought not to retaliate or render evil for evil to any one, whatever evil we may have suffered from him.
divergences.lectio: Then one must not do wrong in return, or do harm to any human being, whatever one suffers at their hands.
divergences.note: Jowett's 'render evil for evil' borrows the wording of the New Testament. Plato has two plain verbs, 'do wrong in return' and 'do harm', built on the same verbs as the steps before, and the edition repeats them so that the argument can be followed link by link.

divergences.older: Leave me then, Crito, to fulfil the will of God, and to follow whither he leads.
divergences.lectio: Then let it be, Crito, and let us act in this way, since this is the way the god leads.
divergences.note: Jowett adds 'to fulfil the will of God', which is not in the Greek. The last sentence of the dialogue says only 'let it be', 'let us act in this way', and that the god leads this way. 'The god' is unnamed, as it is at the end of the Apology.
